does: Cuts food into flat pieces of one thickness.

intro.what: Slicing cuts food into flat pieces of consistent thickness with a forward-and-down stroke.
intro.why: It teaches you to guide the blade smoothly instead of crushing food with downward pressure.

how: Give the food a flat side to rest on.
Hold it with your fingertips tucked back and your knuckles against the side of the blade.
Push the knife forward and down in one stroke, and let its length do the cutting.
Move the guiding hand back by the thickness of a slice after each cut.

cues.text: Slices of the same thickness from the first to the last.
A quiet stroke. A knock on the board at every cut means you are chopping down, not slicing forward.

mistakes.mistake: Pressing straight down, which crushes soft food such as a tomato.
mistakes.fix: Slide the blade forward as it goes down. Sharpen it if it still crushes.

mistakes.mistake: Slices that grow thicker as the hand tires.
mistakes.fix: Slow down. Even matters more than fast.

quiz.question: What is the main aim of slicing evenly?
quiz.because: Consistent cuts give the slices a predictable shape rather than an uneven chopped texture.

quiz.question: How should the blade move through the food?
choices: Straight down with repeated heavy pressure.
Forward and down in a smooth stroke.
quiz.because: Using the length of the blade cuts more smoothly than forcing the edge straight downward.

quiz.question: What might a repeated knock on the board suggest?
choices: The blade is moving quietly forward through the food.
A downward chopping action rather than a smooth slicing stroke.
quiz.because: The sound can reveal a hard downward movement instead of a controlled sliding cut.

quiz.question: Soft tomato is being crushed rather than sliced. What should change?
choices: Slide forward as you cut and check blade sharpness.
quiz.because: A sliding sharp edge cuts the skin and flesh with less crushing pressure.
